claims.statement: As described second-hand in a 2018 narrative review of ketamine pharmacology, whose figures are taken from the primary studies it names and have not been appraised here, ketamine's best-characterised action is to block the NMDA receptor, one of the receptors for the brain's main excitatory messenger: it sits inside the open channel at the phencyclidine site, with a trapping capability of about 86% against more than 98% for phencyclidine and 100% for MK-801. Reported affinities for the racemic drug span Ki 0.18 to 3.1 micromolar across about twenty studies, almost all in rodent tissue, cell lines or frog eggs, with two human post-mortem cortex values of 0.42 and 0.67 micromolar; which receptor subunits are blocked most depends on how much magnesium is present, and one study found no subunit difference at all. A 40-minute infusion of the kind used to treat depression was estimated to occupy at most 31% (SD 18) of the receptors. Most other targets the review tabulates, among them nicotinic, muscarinic, opioid, sigma and monoamine transporter sites and sodium, calcium and HCN1 channels, act at about 10 to 1000 micromolar, above the blood levels reached in people (about 0.8 micromolar after that infusion, about 5 to 10 micromolar at anaesthesia), with exceptions such as one nicotinic receptor blocked at 0.24 micromolar in frog eggs. The body turns ketamine into norketamine, mainly through the liver enzymes CYP2B6 and CYP3A4, and then into dehydronorketamine and the hydroxynorketamines; norketamine also blocks the NMDA receptor (S-norketamine Ki 1.70 to 2.25 micromolar, the R form about eight times weaker) while dehydronorketamine and the hydroxynorketamines are weak or inactive there. In people given that infusion for depression, peak blood levels were 204.13 ng/mL (SD 101.46) for ketamine at 40 minutes, 73.54 (31.86) for norketamine at 80 minutes, 13.27 (6.92) for dehydronorketamine at 110 minutes and 23.19 (11.88) for one hydroxynorketamine pair at 230 minutes, and total exposure to that metabolite pair exceeded exposure to ketamine itself. How much of this is human evidence is the main point: the receptor numbers are overwhelmingly from animal tissue and from receptors grown in cells, the review states that the brain levels of ketamine and its metabolites in people are not known, the proposal that the hydroxynorketamines carry part of ketamine's antidepressant action rests on rodent experiments almost all from the review's own authors, who hold patents on those metabolites, and the review states that no clinical study of R-ketamine in people with depression had been published and that none had compared the two mirror-image forms with each other or with the mixture. A second narrative review, written for a UK scientific committee, adds that ketamine also blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, may strengthen GABA inhibition, releases dopamine and is a weak opioid agonist, but gives no study for several of these statements, and the first review sets against the dopamine account two human imaging studies that found no change in striatal binding, a human study in which a dopamine blocker did not stop ketamine's psychosis-like effects, and a mouse study finding no activity at any dopamine receptor up to 10 micromolar.
claims.magnitude: Zanos et al. (2018), second-hand: NMDA receptor Ki 0.18 to 3.1 micromolar for racemic ketamine across about twenty studies (human cortex 0.42, SE 0.03, and 0.67, SE 0.15); trapping capability about 86% against more than 98% for phencyclidine and 100% for MK-801; estimated maximum receptor occupancy after a 40-minute 0.5 mg/kg infusion 31% (SD 18), against 32% (SD 6) estimated in rats; S-norketamine Ki 1.70 to 2.25 micromolar and R-norketamine 13.0 to 26.46; (2S,6S)-hydroxynorketamine about 10.4 to 21.0 micromolar and (2R,6R)-hydroxynorketamine above 100, neither inhibiting NMDA currents up to 10 micromolar; most other targets 10 to 1000 micromolar, the exceptions including a nicotinic receptor at IC50 0.24 micromolar in frog eggs; human peak blood levels after that infusion 204.13 ng/mL (SD 101.46) ketamine, 73.54 (31.86) norketamine, 13.27 (6.92) dehydronorketamine and 23.19 (11.88) for the (2R,6R;2S,6S)-hydroxynorketamine pair, whose total exposure (1038 and 1366 h.ng/mL in the two patient groups) exceeded that of ketamine (873.5 and 975.4).
